newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Kiev to keep making missiles despite US pressure.
newsitem.headline: Kiev to keep making missiles despite US pressure.

text.p: Ukraine's top security official said on Monday that Kiev would keep manufacturing short- and mid-range missiles for its defence, rejecting pressure from the United States.
Volodymyr Horbulin, secretary of the policy-making Security and Defence Council, also stressed Ukraine had no intention to supply "pariah" countries with its missile technology.
"Missiles with a 300- and 500-kilometre range can be used to defend the borders," Horbulin told reporters. Their production "means preserving jobs and technological potential."
Ukraine has been under pressure from the United States to halt production of the short- and middle-range missiles. Washington fears these missiles could be sold to states like Libya, Iraq and Iran.
"We do not violate any international obligation, any treaty," Horbulin said. "We will never sell -- especially to those countries whose moral standing is in question."
President Leonid Kuchma, who visited Washington last week, has promised the United States he would send SS-24 strategic missiles to Russia for destruction.
Ukraine removed the last strategic nuclear warheads to Russia a year ago but wants to use missiles for space purposes -- a plan opposed by Washington.
"Ukraine is not abandoning the idea of having strategic missiles. Ukraine was, is and will be a space state," Horbulin said. "We cannot give up the products of our brains, knowledge and hands.

"Why should we guarantee that in 2010 we wouldn't produce a missile able to fly to Mars. Maybe it will be a strategic missile ... I don't think that there will be need for this but why should we limit our options?" Horbulin added.
Ukraine produces space, short- and middle-range missiles at the Yuzhmash plant, the world's largest where Kuchma used to be a director, in the eastern industrial city of Dnipropetrovsk.
The United States allocated $47 million this month for the destruction of the strategic missile silos in southern and western Ukraine.
Sources at the State Space Agency said that during Kuchma's visit both sides agreed a Ukrainian cosmonaut would fly aboard the American shuttle in November.
The sources added that the U.S. space agency NASA had chosen Volodymyr Kadenyuk, an ethnic Ukrainian who used to be a Russian air force pilot, for the mission.
